headline: The $60 Shoe That Beat 5 Running Shoes At Disney
script:
My eleven-year-old kept a spreadsheet on our Disney trip last summer. Steps, rides, snacks.

And one column she titled, in capital letters: HOUR MOM SAT DOWN.

This summer she added a new row. What she typed in that box is the reason I'm writing this.

Let me back up. I'm Jenna, forty-three, a dental hygienist in Columbus, Ohio.

I stand all day. I thought I knew shoes.

We saved three years for that first trip. Six days, three parks. Magic Kingdom, Epcot and Animal Kingdom, each one twice.

And because I overprepare for everything, I packed five pairs of shoes. My daughter decided that made it a science experiment.

Day one, Nike Air Max, about $130. Built for gym floors, with a narrow toe box.

Her note for day one: "Hour five. Mom says her feet feel beaten up."

Day two, On Cloud, $180. That triangle-shaped toe box got tight by lunch, with a whole park still to go.

Day three, Hoka. $165, the big ones. For the first two hours, honestly, I was in love.

Then the uneven pavement started, and my foot rolled side to side on all that soft foam. They're heavy, too. By night my knees hurt more than my feet.

Day four, Brooks Ghost, $140. Great for walking. But Disney is an hour standing in line, then walking, then standing again.

Day five, Skechers. $90, and that memory foam feels amazing in the store. By three o'clock it was flat, and my arches were screaming.

Day six I put the Nikes back on and just suffered.

Her spreadsheet ended with an average. Hour Mom Sat Down: four point eight.

Four point eight. On a trip we saved three years for. Whole afternoons of me on a bench holding the bags, watching my family walk off without me.

Here's what bugged me. She'd also logged what we were doing right before I sat. Almost every time: "Line."

Not the walking. The standing.

I showed it to my patient Carol, a mail carrier who's walked the same route for twenty-two years. She laughed and said, "Honey, you packed shoes for runners."

She explained it in about a minute. Running shoes are built for moving forward on a flat road. When you stand still, that soft foam packs flat under you, and nothing's holding your arch anymore.

And in Florida heat, your feet swell all day. So a shoe that fits at nine in the morning is squeezing you by two.

What you need is boring, she said. A wide toe box, arch support built into the shoe instead of foam that flattens, a knit that stretches when you swell, real grip, and light.

Then she lifted her foot onto my chair and said, "Comfort Wear. Sixty bucks."

Sixty dollars. I'd spent over seven hundred dollars on shoes that failed me.

I ordered them that night, mostly to prove her wrong. The first week, honestly, they felt plain. Almost firm, not squishy.

Then I noticed I'd gone a whole Friday of patients without thinking about my feet once.

So this summer, we went back. Same six days, same three parks, one pair of shoes. My daughter rolled her eyes and reopened the spreadsheet.

Day one, twenty-three thousand steps and two hours in line for one ride. My feet didn't hurt less. They didn't hurt.

The knit gave a little in the afternoon, right when my feet started swelling. The arch was still there at ten at night, walking back to the bus.

On the last night she showed me the new row. In the box under Hour Mom Sat Down, she'd typed one word.

"Never."

I'm not the one on the bench anymore. I'm the one in line, still going.

If you've got a trip coming up and a bag full of $165 running shoes, they were built for a track, not a line at Epcot.

headline: 6 Women, 5 Days Of Rain, 1 Shoe That Lasted
script:
I threw a $165 pair of shoes into a trash can outside Animal Kingdom. Soaking wet. Still laced.

My niece fished them out, held them up in the rain, and yelled, "Aunt Wanda, you just lost the bet!"

She was right. Losing that bet is the best thing that's happened to my feet in thirty years.

Let me back up. I'm Wanda, fifty-eight, a school bus driver outside Valdosta, Georgia. Every August before school starts, the women in my family do Disney.

Me, my two sisters, and three of their girls. Six women, five days. And every single afternoon around three o'clock, the sky opens up.

We call it poncho season. You learn to buy the ponchos. Nobody teaches you about the shoes.

Last August my sister Darlene made it a contest. Everybody wear your best walking shoe. Last woman standing gets dinner paid for.

Darlene wore Nike Air Max, about $130. Built for gym floors, narrow in the toe. By hour five she said her feet felt beaten up.

My niece Kayla brought On Cloud, $180. That triangle-shaped toe box got tight by lunch. Then the rain hit, and she still had a whole park to go.

My sister Joyce wore Brooks Ghost, $140. Fine for walking. But we stood an hour in line under a dripping awning, and she shifted foot to foot the whole time.

My niece Mel brought Skechers, $90. That memory foam feels wonderful in the morning. By evening it was flat and soggy, and her arches were throbbing.

And me? I wore the big Hokas, $165. For two hours I was smug.

Then it rained, and the walkways at Epcot turned slick. On that wet, uneven ground, my foot rolled side to side on all that soft foam.

Heavy to begin with, and wet they felt like bricks. By day three my knees hurt more than my feet did.

That was the day I threw them in the trash.

Because one woman in our group never complained. My niece Tasha. She works twelve-hour shifts as a gate agent at the Atlanta airport.

She'd worn the same plain shoes three days straight. Never sat. Never slipped.

And Kayla had bet me twenty dollars, on day one, that Tasha's sixty-dollar shoes would outlast my Hokas.

That night, dripping on a hotel bedspread, I asked Tasha her trick.

She said, "Aunt Wanda, those are runner's shoes. Running is moving forward on a flat road. Disney is standing in line on wet concrete for an hour."

She said when you stand, soft foam packs flat, and your arch has nothing under it. And in August heat your feet swell all day, so a tight shoe just gets tighter.

What she wants at the airport is simple. A wide toe box, arch support built into the shoe, a knit that gives, grip that holds on a wet floor, and light.

Then she held up her foot. "Comfort Wear. Sixty dollars."

Sixty dollars. I'd paid a hundred and sixty-five for a pair now sitting in a trash can.

I ordered them that night and wore them on my bus route that September. Honestly, the first few days they felt plain. Firm, not squishy.

Then I realized I'd finished a whole double route and never once rubbed my arches at a red light.

This August, poncho season came right on time. Three o'clock, downpour, Epcot.

I walked straight through it, feet planted on the wet pavement. The knit gave a little as my feet swelled.

Twenty-one thousand steps, and my feet didn't hurt less. They didn't hurt.

Darlene ended up on the bench. Not me.

Last woman standing gets dinner paid for. This year, that was me.

And Kayla? This time she bet on my shoes. She won again.

If you're packing $165 running shoes for a summer trip, they were built for a dry track, not a wet line at Epcot.

headline: The $60 Shoe I Wish I'd Packed First
script:
On our anniversary cruise, I spent the first night on the balcony with both feet in the champagne bucket.

Not in the champagne. In the ice.

My husband stood in the doorway with the bottle and said, "Sharon, we've got three days at Disney after this. What are we going to do?"

I didn't have an answer. By the end of that trip I did, and it cost sixty dollars.

Let me back up. I'm sixty-six, and I was a bank teller for thirty-one years, standing behind a counter in whatever shoes the dress code allowed.

For our fortieth, Gary booked it all. Four nights on the ship, then three days in the parks. Our daughter Meg would fly in and meet us for the park part.

I did my homework and read every best-shoes-for-Disney list. A cruise means a big suitcase, so I packed five pairs.

On a ship, everything's fine. You walk a few hundred feet to dinner and sit down. It's the port days that tell the truth.

First port, Nike Air Max, about $130. Built for gym floors, not old stone streets. That narrow toe box had me hunting for a bench by hour five.

My feet didn't feel tired. They felt beaten up.

Next port, On Cloud, $180. Beautiful shoe, but that triangle-shaped toe box pinched by lunch, with the whole walk back to the ship still ahead.

The Hokas, $165, felt like heaven on the deck. Flat, smooth. Then I hit the cobblestones in port, and my foot rolled side to side on all that foam.

And they're heavy. Climbing the gangway that evening, my knees hurt more than my feet.

That's the night I ended up in the ice bucket.

I still had two pairs for the parks. Brooks Ghost, $140, and Skechers, $90. I already knew how that would go.

The Brooks are lovely for walking, but Disney is an hour standing in line. And Skechers memory foam always went flat on me by three.

The last night of the cruise, we shared a dinner table with a woman named Pat. Retired flight attendant. Thirty-four years on her feet in a narrow aisle.

She saw me slip my shoes off under the table. She didn't say a word. She just pulled up her pant leg and showed me hers.

Then she said, "Running shoes are built for moving forward on a flat road. Travel isn't that. It's standing, waiting, cobblestones, then standing again."

She told me soft foam packs flat when you stand on it, and then your arch has nothing. And in the heat your feet swell, so a shoe that fit at breakfast pinches by dinner.

Hers had a wide toe box and arch support built into the shoe. A knit that gives when you swell, real grip, and light enough she forgot she had them on.

"Comfort Wear," she said. "About sixty dollars."

Sixty dollars. I had over seven hundred dollars of shoes in my suitcase.

That night I ordered a pair and had them sent to Meg before her flight. She handed them over at the hotel like contraband.

First morning at Magic Kingdom, honestly, they felt plain. Firm, not squishy. I was nervous.

By noon I'd stopped thinking about my feet. By evening at Epcot, we'd done twenty thousand steps, and I was the one asking, "What's next?"

The knit gave as my feet swelled in the afternoon. The arch was still there walking back at ten at night.

My feet didn't hurt less. They didn't hurt.

I wasn't the one on the bench. Gary was, and I teased him about it all the way to Animal Kingdom.

On our last night there was an ice bucket in our hotel room. Gary put a bottle of champagne in it.

That's what it's for.

If you're packing $165 running shoes for a trip you've saved years for, they were built for a track, not a cobblestone street.
